top_story: After Trump’s March threat to strike Iran’s power grid unless Tehran reopened the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian commanders signaled readiness to widen the confrontation, underscoring how quickly energy security and civilian infrastructure had become bargaining chips. The breakthrough announced on 15 June, and formalized in Trump’s 14-point peace plan on 18 June, reverses that trajectory by pairing reopened maritime traffic with the release of blocked Iranian assets and a path to further negotiations. The agreement offers immediate relief to shipping lanes and regional economies already strained by disruption, but it lands amid fierce backlash in both Tehran and Washington, where critics see either capitulation or proof that the earlier coercive campaign was futile. The core takeaway is that both sides stepped back from a crisis they had sharply intensified, yet the deal’s durability will depend less on signatures than on whether domestic opponents can be contained long enough for tangible economic gains to reach affected populations.
